one_liner: 221 kB user-mode x86-64-linux emulator with a splicing JIT; claims up to 2x over qemu-x86_64 on some workloads.
what_it_does: Blink runs x86-64 Linux ELF binaries (static or dynamic), Actually Portable Executables and flat .bin files on another host, the job `qemu-x86_64` does in user mode. It also runs on non-Linux POSIX hosts (macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Cygwin), which qemu-x86_64 does not. The interface is a command line, `blink [FLAG...] PROGRAM [ARG...]`, not a library API. A companion TUI debugger, `blinkenlights`, adds instruction stepping, reverse debugging by scroll wheel, and i8086 real mode.
how_it_is_fast: The JIT builds 'paths' of about 5 guest instructions (about 13 once chained) ending at branches. It does not run a full code generator: generated functions call micro-op functions that the C compiler already built, and Blink copies those function bodies inline after finding their length by scanning for RET, much like selective-inlining or call-threaded JITs. Paths tail-call one another so execution stays out of the interpreter loop, and tight backward branches may loop natively. Guest memory is identity-mapped at a fixed host offset, so each access costs one add instead of a 4-level page walk with a 16-entry TLB (`-m` restores the walk at about 4x slower). Compiled paths are looked up in a lockless hash table read with acquire loads; the README credits this table for using about 40% less peak RSS than QEMU. The JIT also skips computing EFLAGS when it predicts nothing reads them.
when_to_use: Running short-lived x86-64 Linux command-line tools, such as compilers or build steps, on an ARM64 or x86-64 host, where translation start-up dominates; the 2x claim comes from GCC cc1 compiling Hello World.
Running x86-64 Linux binaries on macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD or Cygwin, where qemu-x86_64 user mode is not available.
Shipping a tiny emulator: 221 kB, about 120 kB with optional features disabled, with libc as the only dependency.
Cosmopolitan Libc, musl or Alpine-built binaries, which the README names as the best-supported guests.
Debugging or teaching x86 execution with the blinkenlights TUI, which offers reverse stepping and memory panels.
when_not_to_use: Binaries that need SSE4.1, SSE4.2, AES-NI or AVX/AVX2. blink/cpuid.c leaves those bits clear, so glibc builds that require x86-64-v2 abort with 'CPU does not support x86-64-v2' (open issue #172), and code that dispatches on CPUID falls back to SSE2/SSSE3 paths.
Programs that need 80-bit x87 long double precision: Blink computes x87 in 64-bit double.
Programs that depend on uncommon Linux syscalls (membarrier, timerfd_create (#155), FUTEX_REQUEUE (#183), ptrace, SysV message queues) or on whole-system state (ps, shared mount namespaces).

Long-running, compute-heavy guests where throughput matters more than start-up: no measured suite shows Blink ahead of QEMU in general. Hosts other than x86-64 and aarch64 get only the interpreter, which the README says is about 10x slower than the JIT.
Production use that needs exact emulation: there are open correctness bugs, such as FDIV and FDIVR executed swapped (#196) and data corruption running a Go 1.25 program (#213).

integration.form: standalone executable (blink, blinkenlights) built from C11 source with ./configure && make; no embeddable library API is documented
integration.dependencies: libc (POSIX.1-2017 with XSI extensions); modern GNU Make to build
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler with atomics (README: e.g. GCC 4.9.4+); the source also compiles as C++
integration.platforms: Hosts: Linux (x86, ARM, RISC-V, MIPS, PowerPC, s390x), macOS (x86, ARM), FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Cygwin. The JIT runs only on x86-64 and aarch64 hosts. Guests: x86-64-linux user mode, plus i8086 real mode in blinkenlights.
integration.thread_safety: Multithreaded guests are supported (clone, fork). The JIT hook table is lockless with acquire-ordered reads. set_robust_list is not implemented, so robust mutexes are not released when a thread or process crashes.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it takes the same `emulator PROGRAM ARGS` command shape as qemu-x86_64, but supports a smaller ISA (no SSE4.x, AVX or AES-NI) and a subset of syscalls (150+ per the README, 180 per the 1.0 notes), and the README warns it 'can be picky about which Linux binaries it'll execute'

gotchas: The JIT assumes flags do not flow across CALL and RET (only REP RET carries them), so code that returns a status in EFLAGS computed by arithmetic, such as SUB, can see the wrong flags. Faults raised by PUSH or POP report an imprecise RIP.

With the linear-memory optimization on hosts whose pages exceed 4 KiB (Apple M1 16 KiB, Cygwin 64 KiB), misaligned read-only guest pages can become writable and JIT hooks may not be invalidated on misaligned RWX pages. Unaligned ELF segments fail with 'p_vaddr p_offset skew unequal' unless you pass -m (slower) or relink with max-page-size=65536.
SIGSYS is reserved for Blink's internal signal delivery, so guests cannot receive it from other processes. Running out of the 22 MB JIT arena flushes all compiled code.

Benchmark evidence: the repo has no benchmark harness (test/ holds only asm, blink, flat, func, metal and metalrom), and neither the README nor the 1.0 notes name a QEMU version, CPU or flags. The comparison guests' CPUID also differs (Blink hides SSE4/AVX), so glibc and other dispatching code may run different code paths under each emulator.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Blink over Box64 DynaRec, Instrew or oxtra when the host is not Linux (macOS, BSD, Cygwin), when the guests are short-lived processes such as compiler runs, or when binary size matters. Pick Box64 for broad application compatibility on ARM64 or RISC-V Linux, and Instrew (LLVM-based translation, measured on SPEC CPU2017) for long-running compute workloads where peak throughput matters.
verified_claims_summary: Only first-party claims exist: the README says Blink is 2x faster than qemu-x86_64 on 'some benchmarks, such as SSE integer / floating point math', and the 1.0 notes (2023-06-04) say it compiles Hello World with GCC cc1 'at least 2x faster', shown in one screenshot. No QEMU version, host CPU, compiler flags or benchmark code are published, and no independent measurement was found.
status_note: ISC-licensed, 7.6k stars, but maintained only occasionally: the last commits were on 2025-12-10 (Fil-C support, TUI fixes), after a handful of commits in 2024-2025. 43 issues are open, including open correctness bugs (#196 FDIV/FDIVR swap, #213 Go data corruption). It is usable as a tool, but the speed claim is unmeasured.
